name: dooption
prose: Telnetd handler for a received IAC DO option (state.c:722-818). It first adjusts will_wont_resp[option]: if non-zero it is decremented once, and once more if it is still non-zero and my state for the option is WILL. Only when the counter is then 0 and my want-state is WONT does it run the option switch: ECHO (init_termbuf, tty_setecho(1), set_termbuf), BINARY (tty_binaryout(1) the same way), SGA (turn_on_sga = 0), STATUS and, when compiled in, ENCRYPT are accepted; TM sends WILL with send_will, sets my want-state and my state for TM to WONT and returns immediately; LOGOUT sets want-state and state to WILL, sends WILL LOGOUT, calls netflush and cleanup(0) (the code marks this as not returning); LINEMODE, TTYPE, NAWS, TSPEED, LFLOW, XDISPLOC, the environment options and any other option are not accepted. An accepted option gets my want-state WILL and a WILL; an option that is not accepted increments will_wont_resp[option] and gets a WONT. On every path that does not return early at TM or at cleanup, my state for the option is then set to WILL (also when the counter was non-zero or a WONT was just sent). Returns void.
note: state.c:722-818 read in full (the same function appears in two packet slices; real file lines used). Reviewer 1 and 2 right (TM returns with my state left WONT, 770-773, so the old wording that every returning path sets WILL was wrong).

name: cleanopen
prose: Opens the slave side of a pty for telnetd and returns a descriptor or -1 (sys_term.c:953-1012). If the global ptyslavefd is not -1 it returns that cached descriptor right away, doing nothing else. Otherwise, unless STREAMSPTY is built and really_stream is set, it chowns the line to 0:0 and chmods it to 0600, ignoring failures; with HAVE_REVOKE it calls revoke(line); it then opens line with O_RDWR|O_NOCTTY and returns -1 if that fails. Only in the build conditions that apply to old BSD (not CRAY or hpux, BSD <= 43 and no STREAMSPTY) does it then ignore SIGHUP, call vhangup() if HAVE_VHANGUP (nothing if not), restore SIGHUP to the default and reopen the line, overwriting t without closing the first descriptor and returning -1 if the second open fails (the first descriptor is then left open). Only on CRAY with TCVHUP does it issue the TCVHUP ioctl with SIGHUP ignored, reopen the line with O_RDWR, return -1 if that fails (leaving the first descriptor open) and otherwise close the first descriptor and use the reopened one. It returns t. In a build with neither of those conditional blocks the descriptor from the first open is returned.
note: sys_term.c:953-1012 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (ptyslavefd path returns a shared descriptor, 957-958); reviewer 3 right (vhangup only under HAVE_VHANGUP, 987-988, and the whole hang-up and reopen is itself conditional).

name: printsub
prose: Telnetd diagnostic printer for suboptions (utility.c:535-1134; the packet slice cut the head). Parameters are direction ('<' for received, '>' for sent, 0 for none), a pointer to the suboption bytes and a size_t length. It returns at once, doing nothing, if (diagnostic & TD_OPTIONS) is 0. If direction is non-zero it prints "td: recv suboption " or "td: send suboption "; when length >= 3 it examines the last two bytes and prints "(terminated by ... not IAC SE!)" if they are not IAC SE; it then subtracts 2 from length unconditionally, so for a non-zero direction the length must be at least 2 or the unsigned subtraction wraps around. If the resulting length is less than 1 it prints "(Empty suboption??\?)" and returns without the final "\r\n". Otherwise it switches on pointer[0] and writes a description of the known options (TERMINAL-TYPE, TERMINAL-SPEED, TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL, NAWS, LINEMODE, STATUS, X-DISPLAY-LOCATION, NEW-/OLD-ENVIRON and, when compiled in, AUTHENTICATION and ENCRYPT, with a generic form for others) through output_data; several cases read pointer[1], pointer[2] and later bytes with only partial length checks (for example TERMINAL-TYPE reads pointer[1] with no check). In the STATUS ... IS case it compacts doubled SE bytes inside the caller's buffer (writing to pointer[k]) and recurses with printsub(0, ...) on the inner suboption. After the switch it writes "\r\n". The function returns void, does not free, reallocate or keep pointer.
note: Partly read: utility.c:535-600, 818-870, 975-995, 1005-1134 and a skeleton of the output calls in 575-960; most option-specific bodies (LINEMODE, SLC, ENVIRON, AUTHENTICATION) were not read line by line. Reviewer right: the length >= 4-or-2 precondition in the old prose was wrong because the subtraction at line 578 happens for any non-zero direction regardless of option (the TTYPE reference to pointer[1] has no length check, 587).

name: isprime
prose: Static trial-division primality test (dict.c:77-91) on a size_t p. It loops i from 2 while i < p: it returns 0 as soon as i divides p exactly (i * (p / i) == p), and returns 1 as soon as i * i > p; if the loop ends without either it returns 1. So it returns 1 for p equal to 0, 1, 2 or 3 and for prime p, and 0 for composite p >= 4. The product i * i is not checked for overflow, so p is assumed small enough (for a 32-bit-range p on a 64-bit size_t it cannot overflow). It allocates and locks nothing.
note: dict.c:77-91 read in full. Contract left empty (the earlier formal contracts could not state exact primality). Reviewer 1 (formal contract gives only necessary conditions) is consistent with that.

name: findprime
prose: Static function (dict.c:93-103) that returns a prime-looking odd size_t at or above p. If p is even it adds 1, then repeatedly adds 2 while isprime(p) is 0, and returns p. Results: for p = 0 or 1 it returns 1 (because isprime(1) is 1), for p = 2 it returns 3, and for p >= 2 it returns the smallest odd number >= p that isprime accepts, that is the smallest odd prime >= p. It allocates and locks nothing; p + 1 or p += 2 overflowing size_t is not handled.
note: dict.c:93-103 read in full. Reviewer right that for p < 2 the result is 1, which is not prime (p = 0 gives 1, p = 1 gives 1).

name: process_stream
prose: Static function in Heimdal's kadmin rpc.c (lines 747-1094; the packet slice cut the head) that serves one MIT-style ONC-RPC/GSS kadmin connection; contextp is the Kerberos context, buf/ilen the already-read start of the stream (INSIST(ilen >= 4) at line 769) and sp the stream to read from and write to. It creates three in-memory storages (msg, reply, dreply) and then runs a while(1) loop with no exit other than process termination, so it returns no value to the caller; a client EOF ends the process through krb5_errx(contextp, 0, "client disconnected"), and failed INSIST or CHECK macros, RPG_DESTROY, an unknown GSS procedure and a GSS error (krb5_errx with status 1) also terminate. Each iteration truncates msg, reply and dreply, reads one RPC message (the first iteration using buf/ilen, later ones reading from sp, assembling fragments until the last one) and parses the call header, checking RPC version, program, version and the GSS credential flavor with INSIST. When the GSS context is done it verifies the verifier MIC of the header copy. It then switches on the GSS procedure: RPG_DATA requires privacy service and a completed context matching the handle, unwraps the data, requires the sequence number to equal the credential's and to be greater than the stored one, stores it in dreply, and calls the entry of the procs table (when the index is valid and implemented) with (server_handle, sp, dreply), after which line 928 frees sp with krb5_storage_free (the unwrapped storage sp1 is not freed there) and releases the unwrapped buffer; RPG_INIT and RPG_CONTINUE_INIT run gss_accept_sec_context, and on completion look up the client name and initialise the kadm5 server handle, storing the init result in dreply; anything else terminates. After the switch it frees the per-iteration data, builds the RPC reply (xid, accepted, verifier, success, the dreply contents for data calls) in reply and writes it to sp as one fragment with the LAST_FRAGMENT bit (data.length | LAST_FRAGMENT, 1086-1089), inside an INSIST that the full write succeeded. It does not free msg, reply or dreply.
note: Partly read: rpc.c:738-800, 862-935, 1084-1105 and the INSIST/CHECK/krb5_errx skeleton of 800-1090; the init branch (935-1010) and the reply construction (1020-1080) were not read line by line. Reviewer partly right: the reply is indeed framed and written to sp (1087-1089, so the old prose was right on that), but the RPG_DATA branch does free sp (928), which the old prose did not say; the handler receives sp, not sp1 (926).

name: kadmind_dispatch
prose: Static kadmind request dispatcher (server.c:37-457). Parameters: kadm_handlep (a kadm5_server_context), the initial flag, in (the request) and out (the response). It zeroes *out, resolves the caller name into a local buffer, wraps in in a new storage sp (krb5_errx exit on allocation failure), and reads an int32 opcode cmd from it. For each known opcode (get, delete, create, modify, rename, chpass, chpass_with_key, randkey, get_privs, get_princs) it reads the arguments from sp, unparses the principal names, and checks the ACL (_kadm5_acl_check_permission) where applicable; a failure at one of these steps goes to the fail label. Otherwise it calls the matching kadm5 function, frees sp and builds the response in a new in-memory storage that holds the kadm5 return code followed by any result data (for example the principal entry for get). For an unknown opcode it logs, replaces sp with a storage holding KADM5_FAILURE and continues. After the switch it converts sp to *out with krb5_storage_to_data, frees sp and returns 0. So the function returns 0 even when the kadm5 operation itself failed (the failure code is inside *out), and returns a non-zero code only through fail: there it logs, seeks sp to the start, stores the error code as an int32, converts sp to *out, frees sp and returns the error. If reading the opcode fails, the code frees sp at line 68 and then jumps to fail, which uses and frees sp again (server.c:68-69 and 452-455). The caller owns the data in *out and must free it; the function keeps no reference to in.
note: Partly read: server.c:36-101 and 438-457 plus a grep skeleton of the per-opcode code (the argument parsing and ACL branches of 102-438 were not read line by line). Reviewer partly right: sp is a local storage created from in (62), not something supplied by the caller, and it is freed by the function; the old claim that every error returns a non-zero code with the error in *out is true only for the fail path, while kadm5 operation errors are returned inside *out with return value 0.

name: kcm_access
prose: Permission check for a KCM operation on a credential cache (acl.c:38-144; client is a kcm_client, opcode the operation, ccache the cache, and KCM_ASSERT_VALID is applied to ccache). It classifies the opcode as a write (INITIALIZE, DESTROY, STORE, REMOVE_CRED, SET_FLAGS, CHOWN, CHMOD, GET_INITIAL_TICKET, GET_TICKET, MOVE_CACHE, SET_DEFAULT_CACHE, SET_KDC_OFFSET) or a read (NOOP, GET_NAME, RESOLVE, GEN_NEW, RETRIEVE, GET_PRINCIPAL, the UUID-list and by-UUID getters, GET_DEFAULT_CACHE, GET_KDC_OFFSET); any other opcode gives KRB5_FCC_PERM. If the cache has KCM_FLAGS_OWNER_IS_SYSTEM then INITIALIZE, DESTROY, REMOVE_CRED and MOVE_CACHE give KRB5_FCC_PERM, and for any other opcode a root client is permitted (result 0) without looking at the mode, which covers writes as well as reads. Otherwise it builds a mask starting from S_IROTH|S_IWOTH, adds the relevant read or write bits for root (user, group and other), for a client in the same session as the cache (other bits), for the owning uid (user bit) and for a matching gid (group bit), and returns 0 if ccache->mode & mask is non-zero, else KRB5_FCC_PERM. On any non-zero return it logs a message through kcm_log (level 2) naming the pid, operation and cache. It does not allocate or free anything.
note: acl.c:38-144 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (root gets through system caches except for the four forbidden operations, 86-100); reviewer 2 right (the root bypass at 97-100 is not limited to reads, even though its comment says reads).

name: kcm_ccache_new_client
prose: Creates or reinitialises the cache name for a KCM client (client.c:87-178) and returns a krb5_error_code, setting *ccache_p only at the end (line 176) on success. If the global name_constraints is non-zero the name must be the client's decimal uid followed by ":" and anything, or exactly the uid; otherwise it returns KRB5_CC_BADNAME unless the client is root. It then calls kcm_ccache_resolve. If that succeeds and the cache's uid or gid differs from the client's and the client is not root it returns KRB5_FCC_PERM at once, without releasing the resolved ccache reference. If resolve fails with something other than KRB5_FCC_NOFILE it returns that error, except that a root client continues when the error is KRB5_FCC_PERM (the code then goes on with an uninitialised ccache variable in the existing-cache branch below). If the cache does not exist (KRB5_FCC_NOFILE) it calls kcm_ccache_new (logging and returning its error on failure) and binds the new cache to the client's uid, gid and session; otherwise it calls kcm_zero_ccache_data, on failure logging, releasing the cache with kcm_release_ccache and returning that error, and on success calls kcm_cleanup_events. It then calls kcm_access with KCM_OP_INITIALIZE; if that fails it releases the cache, calls kcm_ccache_destroy for the name and returns the error. Finally, for a root client it parses a uid from the name with sscanf ("%ld:" then "%ld") and, if getpwuid finds it, calls kcm_chown to that uid and the user's gid (the result of kcm_chown is ignored). It stores the cache in *ccache_p and returns 0.
note: client.c:87-178 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (the permission-mismatch return at 122 leaks the resolve reference); reviewer 2 right (root with KRB5_FCC_PERM from resolve is let through, 123, and a name that is exactly the uid without a colon is accepted, 108-110, so only names with neither form are BADNAME; the old text also omitted the leaked reference and the uninitialised ccache).

name: _kdc_do_digest
prose: KDC handler for a Digest request (digest.c:202-1517, built when DIGEST is defined; this slice is its tail). Arguments are the Kerberos context, the KDC configuration, the DigestREQ, a krb5_data reply, the peer description string from, and a sockaddr. If config->enable_digest is zero it logs and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY immediately, before touching *reply. Otherwise it zeroes *reply and its local structures, opens the HDB keytab, verifies the AP-REQ, checks that the ticket server principal is digest/R@R, fetches server and client entries, decrypts and decodes the inner request, handles it by operation, and at the end encodes the inner reply, encrypts it with the AP-REP subkey and encodes the DigestREP into *reply (the tail shown here: the default case for an unknown operation sets EINVAL and a message and falls into the failed label, supportedMechs fills the flags from config->digests_allowed, then encode, mk_rep, subkey, crypto init, encrypt, encode). Most failing steps set ret and go to the out label, which returns that non-zero ret with *reply empty. The failed label (digest.c:1417-1436) is different: it takes the current error message, and if none is available clears the message and goes to out with the old ret; otherwise it logs "Digest failed with", builds an error inner reply with reason "unknown error" and code EINVAL (ENOMEM from a failed strdup goes to out), and falls through to the normal encoding; because ASN1_MALLOC_ENCODE assigns ret, a successful encoding of such an error reply makes the function return 0 with *reply holding an error DigestREP. Failures of the final encode/encrypt steps (1440-1481) return their error. The out label (1484-1516) closes or frees the auth context, ticket, keytab, crypto, storage, user, server and client entries, zeroes and frees the password, frees the client name and the temporary and decoded structures, and calls krb5_warn when ret is non-zero; it returns ret. NTLM hash or checksum mismatches that go to failed therefore yield a 0 return with an error reply.
note: Partly read: digest.c:202-300, 400-460, 1405-1517 and the goto/return skeleton of the rest (300-400 and 460-1405, covering the init, CHAP, SASL, MS-CHAP and NTLM handling, were not read line by line). Reviewer 1 right (the failed label produces an error reply and the function returns 0 because the encode macro overwrites ret); reviewer 2 right for the NTLM mismatch goto failed paths (1252-1253).

name: _kdc_do_digest
prose: KDC handler for a Digest request (digest.c:202-1517, built when DIGEST is defined; this slice is its head). If config->enable_digest is zero it logs and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY without touching *reply. Otherwise it zeroes *reply and the local structures, logs the peer, resolves the HDB: keytab (failure goes to out), and calls krb5_rd_req on the AP-REQ (failure to out). It checks that the ticket's server principal has first component KRB5_DIGEST_NAME and second component equal to its realm; any mismatch sets EINVAL with the message "Wrong digest server principal used" and goes to out, except that the earlier krb5_ticket_get_server failure goes to out directly. It then fetches the server entry with _kdc_db_fetch (a failure there goes to out without freeing the principal), fetches the client entry and requires the allow_digest flag (KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY otherwise), decrypts and decodes the inner request, and handles it by operation (init, digestRequest for CHAP, SASL-DIGEST-MD5 and MS-CHAP-V2, ntlmInit, ntlmRequest, supportedMechs, or an unknown operation); in the init case a failed asprintf for the channel binding gives ENOMEM, and for CHAP the identifier is built with asprintf whose return value is not checked, only the resulting pointer is tested for NULL. Failing steps set ret (usually) and go to out, which returns it with *reply empty. Some processing failures go to the failed label, which builds an encrypted error reply and, because the encode macro overwrites ret, makes the function return 0 with an error DigestREP. When krb5_store_stringz or similar fails the code calls krb5_clear_error_message before out, so a non-zero return can have no message set. At out it releases the auth context, ticket, keytab, crypto, storage, entries, password (zeroed first), client name and temporary and decoded structures and logs a warning on a non-zero ret. On success it returns 0 with the encoded DigestREP in *reply.
note: Partly read: digest.c:202-300, 400-460 and the grep skeleton; the middle (300-400 and 460-1405) not read line by line. Reviewer 1 mixed: the CHAP identifier asprintf at 438 is followed by a NULL test of the pointer (so ENOMEM is returned when asprintf leaves NULL), but the asprintf return value is not tested, so it depends on the pointer being set to NULL on failure; reviewer 2 right (krb5_store_stringz failures at 401-405, 423-427 and 449-453 clear the error message before going to out).

name: check_tgs_flags
prose: Static function in krb5tgs.c (lines 374-499) that validates the KDC options in b->kdc_options against the presented TGT and sets the matching flags in the new ticket part et; it returns 0 or a Kerberos error code and logs a message on each failure. For validate: it returns KRB5KDC_ERR_BADOPTION if the TGT is not marked invalid or has no starttime, KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_NYV if its starttime is later than kdc_time, else it clears et->flags.invalid; without validate, a TGT with the invalid flag set gives KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_INVALID. Forwardable and proxiable requests require the same flag on the TGT (else KRB5KDC_ERR_BADOPTION) and set it in et; forwarded and proxy requests require forwardable/proxiable on the TGT, set et->flags.forwarded or proxy and copy et->caddr = b->addresses; a TGT that is itself forwarded or proxy passes that flag on. allow_postdate requires may_postdate on the TGT and sets it; postdated requires may_postdate, sets *et->starttime = *b->from only when b->from is non-NULL (et->starttime must be non-NULL for that), sets et->flags.postdated and also et->flags.invalid = 1; without postdated, a b->from later than kdc_time + context->max_skew returns KRB5KDC_ERR_CANNOT_POSTDATE. renewable requires the TGT to be renewable with a renew_till (else BADOPTION), sets et->flags.renewable, allocates et->renew_till with ALLOC (a plain calloc, whose failure is not checked here), calls _kdc_fix_time(&b->rtime) and copies *b->rtime into *et->renew_till. renew requires a renewable TGT with renew_till (else BADOPTION), computes the old lifetime from the TGT's end time minus its starttime (or authtime), sets et->endtime = *et->starttime + old_life, and lowers it to *et->renew_till when that pointer is non-NULL. The function modifies et progressively, so on an error return et may already carry changes made for earlier options. It returns 0 when no check failed.
note: krb5tgs.c:374-499 read (comments skipped). Reviewer 1 wrong: ALLOC at kdc/headers.h:110 is only `(X) = calloc(1, sizeof(*(X)))` with no return, so there is no ENOMEM path; a failed allocation would instead be dereferenced at krb5tgs.c:471; reviewer 2 right (the starttime copy is conditional on b->from, 453-454, and invalid is set at 456).

name: my_fgetln
prose: Static line reader in mit_dump.c (lines 100-131) that reads a line from f into the growable buffer *buf (capacity *sz, length *len), a substitute for fgetln. If *buf is NULL it mallocs *sz bytes (2048 if *sz is 0, setting *sz to 2048 in that case) and returns ENOMEM if malloc fails, leaving *buf NULL and *sz and *len unchanged. It then sets *len to 0 and loops on fgets(&(*buf)[*len], *sz, f). A line is complete, and the function returns 0 with *len = strlen(*buf), when strcspn(*buf, "\r\n") is non-zero (a CR or LF occurs after at least one character, so a buffer starting with a newline does not count) or feof(f) is true. If the data read does not complete a line it adds the length read to *len, grows the buffer with realloc by half (*sz += *sz >> 1), and reads again; the size passed to fgets is *sz rather than the space left after *len, so it can exceed the remaining space. If realloc fails it frees the old buffer, sets *buf to NULL and *sz and *len to 0 and returns ENOMEM. If fgets returns NULL (EOF or error) the function returns 0 without clearing the buffer: *len is 0 if nothing was read in this call, and the previous contents of *buf stay as they were; a final partial line followed by EOF can also end this way with *len being the accumulated length. The caller owns *buf and must free it.
note: mit_dump.c:100-131 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (initial malloc failure leaves *sz and *len unchanged, 106-108); reviewer 2 right (the failed malloc also leaves *buf NULL); reviewer 3 right (a leading newline does not satisfy strcspn(...) != 0 at 114).

name: mit_prop_dump
prose: Reads a kdb5_util dump file and propagates each principal (mit_dump.c:133-209). arg is a struct prop_data, file the path. If fopen fails it returns errno. Otherwise it sets ret to ENOMEM, creates an in-memory storage and loops while my_fgetln returns 0. For each line it counts lineno; a line starting with "kdb5_util" must read "kdb5_util load_dump version N.0" with N of 4, 5 or 6, otherwise errx(1, "line %d: unknown version", ...) or errx(1, "unknown dump file format ...") ends the process immediately without freeing the file, buffer or storage; policy lines are skipped with a warning; lines not starting with "princ" are skipped with a "not a principal" warning; principal lines are converted (_hdb_mit_dump2mitdb_entry, krb5_storage_to_data, _hdb_mdb_value2entry) and passed to v5_prop, the entry freed with hdb_free_entry after the v5_prop call, and any failing step breaks out of the loop with its error in ret. Because my_fgetln returns 0 at end of file without clearing the buffer, the loop does not stop at EOF: it re-parses the last line read again and again until some step fails, so the function does not return 0 in practice. After the loop (reached with ret non-zero, from a failing step, my_fgetln's ENOMEM, or a failed krb5_storage_emem) it closes the file, frees the line buffer and the storage, and ends the process: ret equal to ENOMEM gives errx(1, "out of memory") with no line number, any other non-zero ret gives errx(1, "line %d: problem parsing dump line", lineno). The final return ret is therefore reached only when ret is 0, which the loop structure does not produce.
note: mit_dump.c:133-209 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (EOF returns 0 from my_fgetln without clearing the buffer, 130, so the last line is reprocessed); reviewer 2 right (ENOMEM exit has no line number, 204-205); reviewer 3 right (the kdb5_util header errors at 165-177 use different errx messages and exit without freeing).

name: kswitch
prose: Implements the kswitch command (kswitch.c:60-173); argc and argv are unused. If both opt->cache_string and opt->principal_string are given it ends the process with krb5_errx. Interactive mode (opt->interactive_flag): it builds a table, calls krb5_cc_cache_get_first (krb5_err exit on failure), then iterates with krb5_cc_cache_next until it returns non-zero (an enumeration error just ends the loop). For each cache it gets and unparses the principal; if either fails it skips that cache with continue (leaving that cache open and not listed). Otherwise it adds a numbered row (number, principal, cache type) and appends the cache to the ids array. It prints the table, reads a line with readline, converts it with atoi into a size_t i, ends the process if no line was read, if i is 0, or if i is greater than the number of listed caches (a negative number becomes a huge unsigned value and is rejected as too large), takes ids[i-1] as the selection and closes the other listed caches. Principal mode: krb5_parse_name then krb5_cc_cache_match, each ending the process on failure. Cache mode: krb5_cc_get_prefix_ops for opt->type_string (exit if NULL), asprintf "prefix:cache" (exit on NULL result), then krb5_cc_resolve (exit on failure). With none of the options it ends the process with "missing option for kswitch". Finally it calls krb5_cc_switch on the chosen cache, ending the process with krb5_err if that fails, and returns 0. So it returns 0 only after a successful krb5_cc_switch and otherwise terminates the process.
note: kswitch.c:60-173 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (enumeration errors do not exit, 88-96); reviewer 2 right (cache_next just ends the loop); reviewer 3 wrong: i is size_t, so atoi(-1) becomes a large value and is rejected by i > len at 120-121; no underflow of ids[i - 1] is reachable for negative input.

name: yyparse
prose: Bison-generated LALR parser for the ASN.1 compiler grammar (asn1parse.c:1514-2750, one large function; this slice covers its actions and the error-recovery and exit code). It takes no arguments, keeps its state on the yyss/yyvs stacks and uses the globals yychar, yynerrs and yylval. It returns 0 on YYACCEPT (at 1725 and 2703), 1 on YYABORT (end of input during error recovery at 2635, the state stack emptied while popping for the error token at 2692, or a stack that is still full after growing at 1669-1670) and 2 after yyerror("memory exhausted") via yyexhaustedlab, which is reached when the stack has hit YYMAXDEPTH or a stack allocation fails (1637-1651) or the error-message allocation fails (2618). The grammar actions run when a rule is reduced and may have side effects (building the module tree, reporting errors); some of them may end the process, which was not checked here. At yyreturn it discards a pending lookahead and the symbols left on the stack through yydestruct, frees the stack and error message buffer if they were heap-allocated, and returns the result.
note: Partly read: asn1parse.c:1630-1672 and the grep of YYACCEPT/YYABORT/yyexhaustedlab/yyreturn positions; the grammar actions (about 1000 lines) were not read. Reviewers 1 and 2 right: running into the stack depth limit returns 2 through yyexhaustedlab (1640-1641), not 1; only the post-growth overflow check (1669-1670) is a YYABORT. The old claim that some actions call exit(1) was not verified and was removed.

name: length_tag
prose: Static helper (gen_length.c:47-59) returning the number of bytes of a DER tag encoding for the tag number tag, as a size_t. If tag is at most 30 it returns 1. Otherwise it counts how many times tag can be divided by 128 until it reaches 0 and returns that count plus 1: 2 for tags 31 to 127, 3 for 128 to 16383, 4 for 16384 to 2097151, 5 for 2097152 to 268435455 and 6 for 268435456 to 4294967295. It allocates nothing, has no side effects and takes no locks.

The old random-test failure report (tag=86 giving result 2) agrees with the stated range 31..127 giving 2, so that report was against an earlier wording; the reviewer's remark about side effects is covered by the prose.

name: yy_switch_to_buffer
prose: Flex-generated function (com_err lex.c:1300-1329) that makes new_buffer the current input buffer of the scanner. It always starts by calling yyensure_buffer_stack(), which allocates or grows the buffer stack when needed and ends the scanner through YY_FATAL_ERROR if that allocation fails; this happens even when the buffer to switch to is already current. If YY_CURRENT_BUFFER equals new_buffer it then returns without any further change. Otherwise, if there is a current buffer, it stores back into it the saved character (restoring *yy_c_buf_p from yy_hold_char), the buffer position (yy_c_buf_p) and the character count (yy_n_chars); then it sets the current buffer to new_buffer, calls yy_load_buffer_state() (which loads the scanner state from the new buffer) and sets yy_did_buffer_switch_on_eof to 1. It returns no value.

Reviewer 1 right (the same-buffer return skips saving and setting the EOF flag, 1309-1310); reviewer 2 right (yyensure_buffer_stack is called before the comparison, 1308, so the stack may be allocated on the early-return path).

name: _gssapi_wrap_size_arcfour
prose: Computes the largest input size that wraps into at most req_output_size bytes for an arcfour (RC4-HMAC) GSS context (arcfour.c:761-791; the packet slice held only the function, which the earlier name "unnamed" did not give). It calls krb5_crypto_init(context, key, 0, &crypto); if that fails it stores the error in *minor_status and returns GSS_S_FAILURE without touching *max_input_size. Otherwise it calls max_wrap_length_arcfour(ctx, crypto, req_output_size, max_input_size), which writes *max_input_size (for a DCE-style context the request size minus the wrap-token encapsulation length or 0, otherwise a value computed from the token length and masked to a multiple of 8, or 0); the code treats a non-zero return from it as an error, storing it in *minor_status, destroying the crypto handle and returning GSS_S_FAILURE (the function body read returns only GSS_S_COMPLETE, so that branch is not reached in practice). On success it destroys the temporary crypto handle and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE; *minor_status is not set on success. conf_req_flag and qop_req are not used. The crypto handle is destroyed on every path where it was created, and nothing is returned to the caller beyond *max_input_size and *minor_status.

name: _gss_DES3_get_mic_compat
prose: Decides whether a GSS context needs the old DES3 MIC compatibility behaviour (compat.c:84-106); the caller is expected to hold ctx->ctx_id_mutex. If COMPAT_OLD_DES3_SELECTED is already set in ctx->more_flags it returns 0 without changing anything. Otherwise it calls check_compat for the "broken_des3_mic" list of the [gssapi] config section with match value TRUE and then, regardless of the first result unless it returned an error, for the "correct_des3_mic" list with match value FALSE. check_compat parses each listed principal and, for the first one that matches ctx->target, sets use_compat to its match value and stops; a parse failure makes it return GSS_S_FAILURE and store the krb5 error in *minor_status when minor_status is non-NULL. If either call returns an error that error is returned at once and no flag is changed. Otherwise the function sets COMPAT_OLD_DES3 in ctx->more_flags when use_compat is TRUE, always sets COMPAT_OLD_DES3_SELECTED on this path, and returns 0. A "correct_des3_mic" match therefore overrides an earlier "broken_des3_mic" match (use_compat becomes FALSE), and with no match in either list COMPAT_OLD_DES3 is not set.

Reviewer 1 right (a correct_des3_mic match prevents COMPAT_OLD_DES3, and the failure comes from the principal parse, 54-56 and 70-73); reviewer 2 right (the correct_des3_mic list is consulted after the broken list and overrides it, 96-97 with match_val FALSE).

name: gsskrb5_initiator_ready
prose: Finishes an initiator security context (init_sec_context.c:273-305). It reads ctx->flags, then frees ctx->kcred with krb5_free_creds and sets it to NULL. It closes ctx->ccache with krb5_cc_close only when CLOSE_CCACHE is set in ctx->more_flags, but sets ctx->ccache to NULL in either case. It reads the remote sequence number from ctx->auth_context (the return value is ignored), calls _gsskrb5i_is_cfx(context, ctx, 0), which can update ctx->more_flags, and takes IS_CFX from more_flags. It then calls _gssapi_msg_order_create for ctx->order; if that returns an error it returns that error immediately (with *minor_status set by the callee), leaving ctx->state without INITIATOR_READY and OPEN unset, while kcred and ccache have already been released and more_flags may already have been changed by the CFX step. On success it sets ctx->state = INITIATOR_READY, sets OPEN in ctx->more_flags and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE; *minor_status is not set by this function on success.

Reviewer 1 right (ccache is closed only when CLOSE_CCACHE is set, 286-288, although the pointer is cleared unconditionally); reviewer 2 right (ccache NULLed unconditionally and _gsskrb5i_is_cfx may modify more_flags before the failure return, 292-299).

name: init_auth
prose: Static first-step helper of gss_init_sec_context for the Kerberos mechanism (init_sec_context.c:376-506; arguments include the credential, the context ctx, target name and the time requested). It sets *minor_status = 0 and *actual_mech_type (if non-NULL) to GSS_KRB5_MECHANISM. If cred is NULL it opens the default ccache into ctx->ccache and sets CLOSE_CCACHE (failure returns GSS_S_FAILURE through the failure label), otherwise it uses cred->ccache. It gets the principal of the ccache into ctx->source, sets the default enctypes from cred, reads the ccache "realm-config" data to decide whether DNS canonicalisation is allowed, and calls gsskrb5_get_creds (retrying once with DNS canonicalisation when the first call failed and DNS is allowed); a failure there goes to failure with the status from gsskrb5_get_creds. It records ctx->lifetime from the credentials' end time, calls _gss_DES3_get_mic_compat and _gsskrb5_lifetime_left (failures go to failure with their status), and if the remaining lifetime is 0 it sets *minor_status = 0 and fails with GSS_S_CONTEXT_EXPIRED. It then sets the auth context key to the session key and generates a local subkey; a failure there returns GSS_S_FAILURE via failure. On success it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with ctx holding ccache, source, kcred and lifetime. The failure label closes ctx->ccache only if it is set and CLOSE_CCACHE is set, sets ctx->ccache to NULL in every case, and returns the stored status; the status can therefore be one returned by a helper, not only GSS_S_FAILURE, and other fields such as ctx->source and ctx->kcred remain as they were.

Reviewer 1 right (the expired-lifetime failure sets *minor_status = 0, 479); reviewer 2 right (ccache NULLed unconditionally, 502, and failure statuses may come from helpers, 455-476).

name: _gsskrb5_set_sec_context_option
prose: Public Kerberos-mechanism implementation of gss_set_sec_context_option (set_sec_context_option.c:101-260; helper functions get_bool, get_string, get_int32 and set_int32 at 40-99). It initialises the Kerberos context with GSSAPI_KRB5_INIT. If value is GSS_C_NO_BUFFER it sets *minor_status = EINVAL and returns GSS_S_FAILURE. It then dispatches on desired_object. DES3 MIC compat: returns GSS_S_NO_CONTEXT (minor EINVAL) when *context_handle is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT; get_bool fails with GSS_S_FAILURE and minor EINVAL when value->value is NULL or the length is not 1; otherwise under ctx->ctx_id_mutex it sets or clears COMPAT_OLD_DES3 and sets COMPAT_OLD_DES3_SELECTED and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE without setting *minor_status. DNS canonicalize: same get_bool checks, then krb5_set_dns_canonicalize_hostname and GSS_S_COMPLETE without setting *minor_status. Register acceptor identity: get_string (malloc failure gives GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE with minor 0), then the result of _gsskrb5_register_acceptor_identity (an empty value passes NULL). Set default realm: get_string, GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_READ (minor 0) for an empty string, otherwise krb5_set_default_realm whose return value is ignored, and GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. Send-to-KDC: an empty value clears the callback; otherwise the length must equal sizeof(struct gsskrb5_send_to_kdc) (else GSS_S_FAILURE with minor EINVAL), then the function is installed; returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. ccache name: get_string, CALL_INACCESSIBLE_READ for an empty value, krb5_cc_set_default_name with its error placed in *minor_status (GSS_S_FAILURE if non-zero, else GSS_S_COMPLETE). Set time offset: get_int32 (an empty value is accepted, a wrong length gives GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE), then krb5_set_real_time; returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. Get time offset: writes the difference between krb5 time and time(NULL) into the caller's buffer with set_int32 (a wrong length gives GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE) and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. Plugin register: length must equal sizeof(struct gsskrb5_krb5_plugin) (else GSS_S_FAILURE, minor EINVAL), then krb5_plugin_register and GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. Any other OID returns GSS_S_FAILURE with minor EINVAL.

Reviewer 1 right (krb5_set_default_realm's result is ignored, 173); reviewer 2 right (get_bool returns GSS_S_FAILURE with EINVAL for a NULL value->value or length != 1, 44-46, in the DES3 and DNS branches). The old prose also left out the GET_TIME_OFFSET option.

name: gss_authorize_localname
prose: Public GSS function (gss_authorize_localname.c:115-164) that asks whether the (imported) name gss_name may log in as the local user gss_user. It sets *minor_status = 0 first, and returns GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_READ if either name is GSS_C_NO_NAME. It then calls mech_authorize_localname, which walks the mechanism names of gss_name and calls each mechanism's gm_authorize_localname (skipping mechanisms without one, recorded as GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE) and stops at the first result other than GSS_S_UNAUTHORIZED; with no mechanism names the result is GSS_S_NAME_NOT_MN. If that result is GSS_S_COMPLETE the function returns GSS_S_COMPLETE; any result other than GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE (including UNAUTHORIZED and errors) marks mechAvailable. It then calls attr_authorize_localname, which returns GSS_S_BAD_NAMETYPE unless the user name type is GSS_C_NT_USER_NAME and otherwise reads the local-login-user attribute of gss_name, returning GSS_S_COMPLETE when an authenticated value matches the user name bytes, GSS_S_UNAUTHORIZED when it does not, or an error from gss_get_name_attribute (GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE if no attribute value was tried); the function returns that result directly if it is GSS_S_COMPLETE or GSS_S_UNAUTHORIZED. Otherwise, if no mechanism SPI gave an answer (mechAvailable is 0), it calls gss_compare_name and returns GSS_S_UNAUTHORIZED when the call succeeds with no match, GSS_S_COMPLETE when it succeeds with a match, or the error status of the compare. If a mechanism did answer but neither it nor the attribute authorised, the status from the attribute step (for example GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE or GSS_S_BAD_NAMETYPE) is returned. *minor_status may be overwritten by the subordinate calls and is not guaranteed to be 0 on return.

name: _gss_ntlm_init_sec_context
prose: NTLM mechanism implementation of gss_init_sec_context (ntlm/init_sec_context.c:219-503; the packet name was wrong). At entry it sets *minor_status = 0, *ret_flags and *time_rec (when non-NULL) to 0 and *actual_mech_type (when non-NULL) to GSS_C_NO_OID. If *context_handle is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT (first call) it callocs a context (failure: *minor_status = EINVAL and GSS_S_FAILURE with no context created), stores it in *context_handle, copies the supplied credential or obtains one for the target name (failure: the context is deleted through _gss_ntlm_delete_sec_context, *minor_status is set to the error and GSS_S_FAILURE returned), builds the NTLM type 1 negotiation flags from req_flags, encodes a type 1 message with the target domain (an encoding failure deletes the context and returns GSS_S_FAILURE with that error) and returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED with the new token in output_token, which the caller must release; actual_mech_type, ret_flags and time_rec keep their entry values on this return. On later calls it decodes input_token as the type 2 message (failure: context deleted, GSS_S_FAILURE with the error), builds a type 3 message (random nonce, NTLMv2 session or NTLM response, LM/NTLM data, session key; failures delete the context and return GSS_S_FAILURE with *minor_status set to EINVAL or the callee's error), installs the session key into the context (v2 or RC4 state, STATUS_SESSIONKEY), encodes the type 3 message (freeing the temporary type 3 buffers; an encoding failure again deletes the context), places it in output_token, sets *actual_mech_type = GSS_NTLM_MECHANISM, *ret_flags = 0 and *time_rec = GSS_C_INDEFINITE when the pointers are non-NULL, sets STATUS_OPEN and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE. *minor_status stays 0 on the two successful return codes. On failure output_token is not written.

Reviewer: only the mechanical name rejection was recorded; the function exists under the name _gss_ntlm_init_sec_context. The old prose said *minor_status is not written on success, which is wrong because it is set to 0 at line 238.

name: acceptor_complete
prose: Static SPNEGO acceptor helper (accept_sec_context.c:405-466; the packet slice was in the middle of the file) called when the underlying mechanism step finished. It calls _gss_spnego_require_mechlist_mic(minor_status, ctx, &require_mic) and returns its error if non-zero. It stores that value in ctx->require_mic and only afterwards, if mic is non-NULL, sets the local require_mic to 1 (so ctx->require_mic is not forced on by mic). If ctx->open is set and require_mic is true it decides the MIC handling: with mech_input_token equal to GSS_C_NO_BUFFER it sets verify_mic to 1 and *get_mic to 0; else if mech_output_token is non-NULL with length 0 it sets both to 1; otherwise verify_mic is 0 and *get_mic is 1. In each of these cases it DER-encodes ctx->initiator_mech_types into a newly allocated mech_buf->value (the caller owns it; an encoding failure sets *minor_status and returns GSS_S_FAILURE, and a length mismatch is an internal heim_assert). If verify_mic is set it calls verify_mechlist_mic; on error it calls send_reject(minor_status, output_token) only if *get_mic is also set and returns that error; on success it sets ctx->verified_mic = 1. If the context is not open or no MIC is required it sets *get_mic to 0 and skips the rest. Otherwise it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE.

name: acceptor_continue
prose: Static SPNEGO acceptor step for the second and later tokens (accept_sec_context.c:689-873), taking the usual gss_accept_sec_context arguments; *context_handle must already hold a gssspnego_ctx. It decodes input_token_buffer as a NegotiationToken; if decoding fails it sets *minor_status to the error and returns GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN, and if the token is not a negTokenResp it sets *minor_status = 0 and returns GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN; both returns happen before the context mutex is taken and without deleting the context or invalidating the handle. It then locks ctx->ctx_id_mutex and, if a responseToken is present, releases any earlier mech_src_name and calls gss_accept_sec_context with it on the negotiated context; a result other than GSS_S_COMPLETE or GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED frees the token, sends a reject token with send_reject, unlocks the mutex and returns that result at once, again without deleting the context; GSS_S_COMPLETE sets ctx->open = 1. It then calls _gss_spnego_require_mechlist_mic and stores the answer in ctx->require_mic; with a COMPLETE inner result it calls acceptor_complete (MIC handling), determines require_response for DCE-style contexts, and, if there is a non-empty mechanism output token, or the context is open and the peer's negResult is accept_incomplete, or a response is required, or a MIC must be sent, it calls send_accept to fill output_token. A failure of the require_mechlist_mic or send_accept calls (ret2) replaces ret. It releases the mechanism output token and mech_buf and frees the decoded token. On GSS_S_COMPLETE it moves the mechanism source name into a newly allocated spnego_name for *src_name when requested (if that allocation fails *src_name is simply not set). It sets *mech_type, *ret_flags and *time_rec from the context when the pointers are non-NULL, and returns ret with the mutex unlocked when ret is GSS_S_COMPLETE or GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED; for any other final result it calls _gss_spnego_internal_delete_sec_context on the handle and returns ret.
note: accept_sec_context.c:689-873 read in full except comment lines. The packet had marked this item dropped; the function exists and is fixed. Reviewer right (the early DEFECTIVE_TOKEN returns at 725-731 do not delete the context or clear the handle; also the reject path at 776-781 returns without deleting it). Not read: send_accept, send_reject, _gss_spnego_internal_delete_sec_context (so how the mutex is released on the delete path is not stated).

name: ca_sign
prose: Static function in hx509 ca.c (lines 983-1422; the earlier name build_tbs_certificate does not exist in this file, and the function both builds and signs the certificate) that builds a certificate from the template tbs, signs it with signer and stores the result in *certificate; issuername and ai (authority key identifier) may be NULL. It first fixes the validity (notBefore defaults to one day before now, notAfter to one year after now) and the key usage (default digitalSignature|keyEncipherment, plus keyCertSign|cRLSign for a CA). It then returns EINVAL with an error string, before allocating anything, if tbs->flags.key is 0, if the template is not a proxy and has no subject name or a null subject with no subjectAltNames, if both ca and proxy are set, or if a proxy template has subjectAltNames. Otherwise it fills a local Certificate: version 3; a serial number copied from tbs->serial when flags.serial is set, else 20 random bytes with the top bit of the first byte cleared (the RAND_bytes result is not checked); the default signature algorithm; the issuer (a copy of issuername, or the subject name when issuername is NULL); the validity; the subject (a proxy prefix built from the issuer for proxy templates, else the template subject); the subject public key info; optional issuer and subject unique IDs; and extensions (the domainController marker if flagged, KeyUsage, ExtendedKeyUsage when tbs->eku.len > 0, subjectAltName when tbs->san.len > 0, AuthorityKeyIdentifier when ai is non-NULL, a SHA-1 SubjectKeyIdentifier of the public key, BasicConstraints (critical for CA), ProxyCertInfo for proxy templates, and CRL distribution points when present). It DER-encodes the TBSCertificate (a size mismatch ends in _hx509_abort), signs it with _hx509_create_signature_bitstring and wraps the result with hx509_cert_init into *certificate. Any allocation, copy, encoding, signing or init failure goes to the out label, which frees the local Certificate and returns the error code (ENOMEM for the local allocations, otherwise the callee's code); on success the local Certificate is freed and 0 is returned. The caller keeps ownership of *certificate only on success.

name: main
prose: Entry point of ipropd-slave (ipropd_slave.c:492-748). It parses options with getarg; a parse failure calls usage(1), --help calls usage(0), and --version prints the version and calls exit(0). It then initialises the Kerberos context (errx exit on failure), installs the signal handlers, builds a default kdc.conf path if none was given (errx on out-of-memory), loads the configuration files (krb5_err exit on failure), requires exactly one remaining argument (the master host, otherwise usage(1)), optionally daemonizes, opens the pidfile and log, registers the HDB keytab, parses the lost-server time (krb5_errx exit if it is negative), initialises kadm5 with the admin service and the log, obtains credentials and the server principal; each of these failures ends the process with a non-zero status through errx, krb5_err or krb5_errx. It then loops while exit_flag is zero: it sleeps until the reconnect delay has elapsed, connects to the master (a failed connect goes to retry), frees any previous auth context and refreshes the ccache, runs krb5_sendauth with mutual authentication (failure: warn and retry), and calls ihave (failure: retry). While connected and exit_flag is zero it checks fd < FD_SETSIZE (krb5_errx exit otherwise), waits in select for up to time_before_lost seconds (an EINTR result continues the loop, another negative result ends the process with krb5_err, and a timeout with no data ends the process with krb5_errx), reads a private message (failure: warn and mark disconnected), and by command code handles FOR_YOU (receive, then ihave, disconnecting if ihave fails), TELL_YOU_EVERYTHING (receive_everything, disconnecting on failure) and ARE_YOU_THERE (send_im_here); all other codes are ignored with a warning. At the retry label it logs, closes master_fd if it is not negative and increases the reconnect delay by backoff up to reconnect_max. After the loop ends (exit_flag set by a signal) it logs the reason (SIGXCPU, SIGINT or SIGTERM, or an unexpected value) and returns 0. The return 0 is therefore reached only after exit_flag becomes non-zero.
note: ipropd_slave.c:492-748 read in full (comment lines skipped; the first 20 lines of declarations omitted). Reviewer right (a select failure with EINTR continues the loop at 675-676 instead of terminating). The packet slice cut the head; the function is main.

name: try_two
prose: Static probe (afssys.c:386-402, compiled only when AFS_PIOCTL is defined) that tests whether the pair syscall_pioctl and syscall_setpag are the AFS pioctl and setpag system calls. It zeroes a struct ViceIoctl and calls setjmp(catch_SIGSYS) itself (so the caller does not set the jump target); on the direct return of setjmp it issues syscall(syscall_pioctl, 0, VIOCSETTOK, &parms, 0, ...) with the remaining arguments zero, ignoring the syscall's return value, and then tests errno without clearing it first: if errno equals EINVAL it sets the global afs_entry_point to MULTIPLE_ENTRY_POINT, afs_syscalls[0] to syscall_pioctl and afs_syscalls[1] to syscall_setpag, and returns 0. In every other case it returns 1 and leaves those globals unchanged: when errno is not EINVAL, or when the probe raised SIGSYS and the signal handler longjmped back (setjmp returning non-zero). Because errno is not reset before the call, an EINVAL value already present before the probe is also treated as success.

name: krb5_acl_match_file
prose: Public function (acl.c:244-295; the slice held only its body) that checks whether any line of the ACL file file matches the printf-like format and its variadic arguments. It opens the file; if fopen fails it saves errno, sets a Kerberos error message "open(file): reason" and returns that errno. It marks the descriptor close-on-exec and calls acl_parse_format(context, &acl, format, ap); if that returns an error it closes the file and returns the error without calling acl_free_list (any message is set by acl_parse_format). It then reads the file with fgets into a 256-byte buffer, skips lines whose first character is '#', and tests each remaining line with acl_match_acl; a non-matching line is followed by free_retv(acl). On the first match it stops with found set. It then closes the file and calls acl_free_list(acl, !found). It returns 0 if a line matched, otherwise it sets the error message "ACL did not match" and returns EACCES. Lines longer than 255 characters are read in pieces by fgets and each piece is matched separately.

name: fcc_move
prose: Moves the file credential cache from onto the cache to (fcache.c:958-1038; the packet slice cut the head). It first calls rk_rename(FILENAME(from), FILENAME(to)). If the rename fails with an errno other than EXDEV it sets a "Rename of file ... failed" error message and returns that errno, closing nothing. If it fails with EXDEV it opens the source for reading (returning the error if that fails, with no other change), unlinks the destination path, opens the destination with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, and copies the data block by block; a short write sets EIO, a read error sets EIO, and a failed destination open also reaches the cleanup. The cleanup unlocks and closes the descriptors and then always erases the source file with _krb5_erase_file (even when the copy failed); if the copy failed it also erases the destination file and returns the error, so a failed cross-device move can leave neither file and the old destination is already gone. When the rename or the copy succeeded it calls init_fcc on the destination cache and, if that succeeds, frees the storage and unlocks and closes the fd it returned. It then calls fcc_close(context, from), ignoring its result (also when init_fcc failed), and returns the result of init_fcc, which is 0 on success.

Reviewer 1 right (the destination is unlinked at 983 before the new one is created, and a failed copy leaves it erased at 1018); reviewer 2 wrong: fcc_close(context, from) is called at line 1035 on every path that reaches it, so the from cache is closed, not just its descriptor. name: krb5_get_forwarded_creds
prose: Builds an encoded KRB-CRED message that forwards a ticket for in_creds, destined for hostname (get_for_creds.c:186-459; the earlier name krb5_mk_cred is not the function in this slice). It first calls krb5_get_credentials(ccache, in_creds): if that succeeds, address lists are used only when the found ticket has addresses; if it fails, address use follows the "no-addresses" app default of the client's realm (an error from that lookup is not examined). When addresses are wanted it resolves hostname with getaddrinfo (failure: sets an error message and returns the translated error) and builds the address list with add_addrs (failure returns its error). It then calls krb5_get_kdc_cred with the flags, frees the address list, and returns its error if it failed. It builds a KRB_CRED with one ticket decoded from the received ticket (a decode or allocation failure releases what was built and returns the error or ENOMEM) and an EncKrbCredPart with one ticket_info; with KRB5_AUTH_CONTEXT_DO_TIME in auth_context->flags it adds the current time and usec; when local_address, local_port and paddrs are all set it adds the sender address and port; when remote_address is set it adds the receiver address (with the port, unless the server realm's "no-addresses" default is true; without a port as a copy of the address). Failures of these steps (ENOMEM or the callee's error) go through the cleanup labels, which free the partially built structures and out_creds and return the error. It then fills the ticket info from out_creds (session key, client and server names and realms, flags, times, addresses) with ALLOC and copy calls whose results are not checked, frees out_creds, and encodes the EncKrbCredPart (an encoding failure frees cred and returns the error). If KRB5_AUTH_CONTEXT_CLEAR_FORWARDED_CRED is set the encoding is stored unencrypted with ENCTYPE_NULL; otherwise it encrypts it with auth_context->keyblock (a failed krb5_crypto_init or encryption frees the buffers and returns the error). It then encodes the KRB_CRED; on success it sets out_data->length and out_data->data to the new buffer (the caller frees it) and returns 0, otherwise it returns the error with out_data unchanged. If an ASN.1 encoder returns a size different from the buffer size the process aborts through krb5_abortx.
note: get_for_creds.c:186-459 read in full, comments skipped. Fixed under the real name since the function exists; the packet's reviewer note was only the mechanical name rejection. One qualification added compared with the old prose: allocation and copy results at 365-385 are not checked.

name: akf_start_seq_get
prose: Starts a sequential read of the AFS keyfile keytab (keytab_keyfile.c:199-235; id->data is a struct akf_data whose filename is opened, c is the cursor). It opens d->filename read-only into c->fd. If the open fails it sets an error message with the errno and returns that errno; c->fd is then -1, and c->data and c->sp are not set. Otherwise it sets c->data to NULL and creates c->sp with krb5_storage_from_fd(c->fd); if that fails it closes the fd, clears the error message and returns KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND. It sets the storage EOF code to KRB5_KT_END and reads a 32-bit entry count into d->num_entries with krb5_ret_uint32. If that read fails, or the count is greater than INT_MAX / 8, it frees c->sp, closes c->fd and clears the error message, and returns KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND when the read error was KRB5_KT_END and otherwise the value of ret, which is 0 when the read succeeded but the count was too large (so in that case the function returns 0 with the cursor's storage freed and the fd closed). On the normal success path it returns 0 with c->sp holding the open storage and c->fd the open descriptor, which the caller must later release through the end-sequence function.
note: keytab_keyfile.c:199-235 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (an unopenable file is handled by returning errno, 206-212); reviewer 2 right (c->fd is set to the failed open's -1 before the return, 206).

name: krb5_krbhst_format_string
prose: Formats a Kerberos host entry as a string (krbhst.c:329-343). It chooses the prefix "tcp/" when host->proto is KRB5_KRBHST_TCP, "http://" when it is KRB5_KRBHST_HTTP and an empty prefix otherwise. If host->port differs from host->def_port it formats ":%d" with the port into a 7-byte local buffer (truncated if the number does not fit). It then calls snprintf(hostname, hostlen, "%s%s%s", prefix, host->hostname, portstr), so the output is the prefix, the host name and the optional port, truncated to hostlen bytes including the terminating NUL when hostlen is greater than 0; with hostlen equal to 0 snprintf writes nothing and hostname is not NUL-terminated by this function. The context argument is unused. It returns 0 on every path; the code has no error return. The caller keeps ownership of hostname and host.
note: krbhst.c:329-343 read in full. Reviewer right (with hostlen == 0 nothing is written to hostname, so no NUL terminator, contradicting the old statement that the result is always NUL-terminated).

name: krb5_rd_req_ctx
prose: Verifies an AP-REQ (rd_req.c:840-1078; the slice and the earlier name krb5_rd_req describe the tail of this function). Parameters: context, a pointer to an auth context (created if *auth_context is NULL), the encoded request inbuf, an optional server principal, an optional input context inctx (keytab, keyblock, check_pac), and outctx (dereferenced at entry). It sets *outctx = NULL, allocates an out context o (ENOMEM with a message on failure), initialises the auth context if needed, decodes the AP-REQ (failures go to out), records the ticket's server name in o->server, and returns KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_NOKEY if the request uses a session key but the auth context has none. The key is taken from the auth context keyblock, else inctx->keyblock (each copied into o->keyblock, copy failures to out), else from the keytab: inctx->keytab or the default keytab (opened into the local keytab variable; a failure of krb5_kt_default is ignored and if no keytab is available the function goes to out with the previous ret, which is 0, so it can return 0 with *outctx holding an out context that has no ticket or keyblock). With a keytab it takes the server from the ticket when none was given, calls get_key_from_keytab, and on its failure goes to out unless the server was derived from the ticket or KRB5_CTX_F_RD_REQ_IGNORE is set, in which case it clears o->keyblock and scans the keytab entries. When it has a keyblock it calls krb5_verify_ap_req2 (failure: out). Otherwise it iterates over the keytab entries, skipping those whose key type differs from the ticket's, skipping entries for which krb5_verify_ap_req2 fails, and on the first success copies the entry's keyblock into o->keyblock and replaces o->ticket->server with a copy of the entry's principal; running out of entries (or a failed start_seq_get) goes to out with the error (including the principal-not-found error); in that failing exit the cursor is not ended. If inctx is NULL or inctx->check_pac is set it then looks for a Windows PAC in the ticket's authorization data and, if present, parses it and verifies it with krb5_pac_verify using the keyblock (a failure goes to out; an absent PAC is not an error). At out, if ret is non-zero it frees o, otherwise it stores o in *outctx (owned by the caller); it frees the decoded AP-REQ, a temporary service principal and the default keytab it opened (the local keytab variable, not a keytab supplied by the caller), and returns ret.
note: rd_req.c:840-1075 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (the slice is krb5_rd_req_ctx with outctx, not krb5_rd_req); reviewer 2 wrong: krb5_kt_close at 1074-1075 is applied only to the local keytab variable, which is set only by krb5_kt_default (907-908), not to the caller-supplied inctx->keytab. Not read: get_key_from_keytab. Note: when an early failure happens before the AP-REQ is decoded (auth context init), free_AP_REQ at 1069 is still called on the uninitialised ap_req.

name: krb5_recvauth_match_version
prose: Server side of the sendauth protocol (recvauth.c:62-226). The auth_context pointer itself must be non-NULL; if *auth_context is NULL it is created with krb5_auth_con_init (failure returned). It sets the addresses from the descriptor p_fd (failure returned) and then, unless KRB5_RECVAUTH_IGNORE_VERSION is in flags, reads a 4-byte length and the sendauth version string; a read error returns errno, an EOF returns KRB5_SENDAUTH_BADAUTHVERS, and a wrong length, short read or different string writes the rejection byte 1 and returns KRB5_SENDAUTH_BADAUTHVERS. No reply byte is written for an accepted sendauth version. It then reads the 4-byte length of the application version (a read error returns errno; EOF returns KRB5_SENDAUTH_BADAPPLVERS without a rejection byte) and mallocs that many bytes, writing the rejection byte 2 and returning ENOMEM if the allocation fails. If krb5_net_read returns a non-zero byte count it NUL-terminates the string if needed and writes the rejection byte 2 and returns KRB5_SENDAUTH_BADAPPLVERS when the count differs from len or match_appl_version(match_data, string) is false; if krb5_net_read returns 0 the match callback is not called and the version is treated as accepted. It frees the string, writes the accept byte 0 (a write failure returns errno), reads the AP-REQ message (error returned) and calls krb5_rd_req; if that fails it tries to send a KRB-ERROR message and returns the krb5_rd_req error (the ticket pointer is not touched). On success it writes a zero 4-byte length (a failure frees and NULLs *ticket and returns errno), and when AP_OPTS_MUTUAL_REQUIRED is set it builds an AP-REP with krb5_mk_rep and writes it, freeing and NULLing *ticket and returning the error if either step fails. It returns 0 with *ticket set to the verified ticket.
note: recvauth.c:62-226 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (most failures return without sending a rejection byte, and auth_context itself is dereferenced); reviewer 2 right (on success no reply is written for the sendauth version, only the application-version accept byte 0 and later messages, and the rejection byte is also sent for an application-version mismatch, 147-150).

name: krb5_string_to_key_derived
prose: Public function (salt.c:249-310; the packet slice held its body) that derives a key for etype from the string str of len bytes using the n-fold and key-derivation method with the well-known constant "kerberos". It looks up the encryption type with _krb5_find_enctype; if it is unknown it sets an error message and returns KRB5_PROG_ETYPE_NOSUPP. It computes keylen as the key type's bits / 8, allocates a key structure kd.key (ENOMEM with a message on failure) and its key value (krb5_data_alloc error returned after freeing kd.key), sets its type, and mallocs a temporary buffer of keylen bytes (on failure frees the key with krb5_free_keyblock and returns ENOMEM). It folds the string into the buffer with _krb5_n_fold; if that fails it frees the temporary buffer and returns the error, without freeing kd.key (leaking it). Otherwise it converts the folded buffer to a key with _krb5_DES3_random_to_key (its result is not checked), zeroes and frees the buffer, and calls _krb5_derive_key with "kerberos"; if that fails it frees the key data with _krb5_free_key_data and returns the error. On success it copies the derived key into *key with krb5_copy_keyblock_contents, frees the temporary key data, and returns the result of the copy (0 on success); *key then holds contents that the caller frees with krb5_free_keyblock_contents. *key is not written before the final copy, so on the earlier failures it is unchanged.
note: salt.c:249-310 read in full. The packet had marked this item dropped as unnamed; the function is krb5_string_to_key_derived and is fixed under that name. Not read: _krb5_n_fold, _krb5_derive_key, _krb5_free_key_data.

name: krb5_sendto
prose: Sends send_data to the KDCs of a host handle and collects the reply in receive (send_to_kdc.c:366-454). It first zeroes *receive. Then it repeats up to context->max_retries times: it walks the hosts of handle with krb5_krbhst_next and for each host tries, in order, (a) a user-installed context->send_to_kdc function, (b) a send_to_kdc plugin (send_via_plugin), (c) for HTTP hosts with context->http_proxy, send_via_proxy, and (d) a direct connection: it resolves the host with krb5_krbhst_get_addrinfo and, for each address, creates a socket, connects, sends over HTTP, TCP or UDP with context->kdc_timeout, and closes the socket. For attempts (a), (b) and (d) a result of 0 with receive->length non-zero ends the function successfully; a failed or empty attempt moves on to the next host or address. For the proxy attempt a return value of 0 alone ends the function with ret 0 (the length of receive is not checked there). After a pass over all hosts it calls krb5_krbhst_reset and retries. If every attempt fails, or max_retries is 0, it clears the error message and returns KRB5_KDC_UNREACH; receive is not zeroed again at that point, so it may hold whatever a failed attempt left in it. On success it returns 0 with receive holding the reply. A debug message with the result is logged on the way out. The function itself does not free receive on failure and does not modify handle beyond iterating and resetting it.

name: krb5_sendauth
prose: Client side of the sendauth protocol (sendauth.c:63-232). It writes the length-prefixed protocol version string and then the application version string to p_fd (a short write returns errno with a message), reads a one-byte reply (a read error returns errno, a short read returns KRB5_SENDAUTH_BADRESPONSE, a non-zero byte returns KRB5_SENDAUTH_REJECTED). If in_creds is NULL it builds a template: it opens the default ccache when ccache is NULL (remembering it must close it; failure returns the error) and takes the client principal from the ccache when client is NULL (a failure closes a ccache it opened and returns the error). If the credentials have no ticket it calls krb5_get_credentials; on failure it closes a ccache it opened and returns the error without freeing the temporary client principal, which leaks; with a ticket present creds is just in_creds. It closes the ccache it opened and calls krb5_mk_req_extended. Then, whether or not that succeeded, it either stores creds in *out_creds (when out_creds is non-NULL) or frees creds with krb5_free_creds (note that this can free the caller's in_creds when it contained a ticket and out_creds is NULL), and frees the temporary client principal; if krb5_mk_req_extended failed it returns that error. It sends the AP-REQ with krb5_write_message (on failure it returns the error and does not free ap_req), frees the request, reads a message from the server with krb5_read_message (error returned) and, if the message is non-empty, decodes it as a KRB-ERROR: it converts it with krb5_error_from_rd_error, stores a malloc'd copy in *ret_error when ret_error is non-NULL (freeing the error contents if the malloc fails), otherwise frees the error contents, and returns the translated code; a decode failure returns that error. If AP_OPTS_MUTUAL_REQUIRED is set it reads the AP-REP message (error returned) and verifies it with krb5_rd_rep, storing the encrypted part in *rep_result or freeing it when rep_result is NULL. It returns 0 after a completed handshake.
note: sendauth.c:63-232 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (ap_req leaks when krb5_write_message fails, 175-179); reviewer 2 right (the temporary principal this_client leaks when krb5_get_credentials fails, 147-152).
